content.text:
I read the "Add Printer Flow" page from Chrome. It's a 1280×800 "Add a printer" dialog shown in six states, each on top of the dimmed Workspace Home screen.

**Why screenshots failed at first:** the Figma tab had frozen, and even a one-line script timed out after 45 seconds. The Chrome extension itself was fine, since it captured example.com right away, so I didn't restart it. I closed the frozen tab and opened the page in a new one, which worked. That new tab is still open.

**18a — Initial.** The user describes their printer and the dialog works from that.
- A text box asks "What printer do you have?". The placeholder suggests loose answers like "bambu a1 mini", "the ender with the touchscreen" or "not sure, it's the small one".
- Below it is a drop zone for a photo of the printer, its nameplate or its box.
- A "Found on your network" list shows each discovered printer with its serial number and a "Use this" button, e.g. Bambu Lab A1 mini.
- The footer has a "Set it up myself" link and a Next button. Next stays disabled until the user types something or drops a photo.

**18b — Recognized.** The agent has identified the printer from the description or photo.
- A card shows the printer's picture, name (Bambu Lab A1 mini) and build volume (180×180×180 mm).
- The agent states its assumptions: "I'll assume a **0.4 mm nozzle**, the **textured PEI plate** it ships with, and **PLA**."
- A correction field sits below, with examples like "I put a 0.6 nozzle on it" or "It's the Combo with the AMS".
- Buttons: "Not this one" and "Add this printer".

**18c — Network Selected.** The user picked a printer found on the network.
- It shows "Found on your network" plus the serial number.
- The card reads nozzle, plate and loaded filament from the printer itself ("AMS lite: Bambu PLA Matte + 3 more"), so the agent has nothing to assume.
- An optional access code field keeps the printer connected. The text says to find the code under Settings › Network on the printer, or to sign in to Bambu instead.

**18d — Ambiguous.** More than one printer matches what the user typed.
- For "the ender with the touchscreen", the dialog explains how to tell the two apart: the Ender-3 V2 has a knob under the screen; the S1 has no knob and a direct-drive extruder.
- Each candidate gets a card with a "This one" button.
- The user can also add a photo ("A photo of the front settles it") or more text ("the box says S1 Pro").
- A "Neither — it's not in the list" link covers the no-match case.

**18e — Set it up myself.** This is the manual path, in a wider dialog.
- A left-side step list: Printer, Filaments, Bed shape, Firmware, plus a "Found on network" shortcut.
- A vendor dropdown (Bambu Lab) above a grid of models: A1 mini, A1, P1S, P1P, X1 Carbon, H2D.
- Each model card has nozzle-size chips (0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6 / 0.8) to tick the nozzles the user owns.
- A "Custom printer" link, an "Ask the agent instead" link at top right, and Cancel / Back / Next buttons.

**18f — No Agent Connected.** Shown when no AI agent is configured.
- A highlighted card says "No agent connected" and explains what the agent would do.
- It has a "Set up the agent" button with the note "About a minute. Your own key, or an AI tool you already use."
- Network discovery with "Use this" still works, and "Or set it up myself from the lists" is still offered.

**Links to other pages.** A note under 18f lists these because they can't be wired as prototype links:
- On the Home screen, "Add Printer" opens 18a when an agent is connected, or 18f when none is.
- In 18f, "Set up the agent" goes to the "Agent Setup · Empty State" page.

1	# JusPrin production architecture
2	
3	**Status:** Selected architecture and production implementation boundary for `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin replaces OrcaSlicer's primary presentation and workflow, while retaining OrcaSlicer's mature manufacturing behavior. Product work must simplify how users express intent and verify a print; it must not fork slicing, geometry, rendering, picking, serialization, or history behavior.
6	
7	## Product composition
8	
9	The target project window has four stable regions:
10	
11	1. A compact machine and project status row.
12	2. A collapsible, thin plates and objects pane.
13	3. OrcaSlicer's existing Prepare or G-code Preview canvas.
14	4. A fixed Agent conversation and print-plan pane.
15	
16	The compact plates/objects pane is deferred to a later task. The first
17	production shell and Agent implementation must not depend on it; users interact
18	with objects through the native canvas and Agent until the pane is added.
19	
20	Prepare is the persistent workspace. **Check print** temporarily replaces its center canvas with Orca's real sliced Preview. **Print** opens Send preflight and never sends immediately. Project details are a drawer, and Monitor is a separate surface that can remain visible during other work.
21	
22	## Runtime architecture
23	
24	```text
25	OrcaSlicer process (C++17 / wxWidgets / OpenGL)
26	├── JusPrin application shell
27	│   ├── compact top navigation and machine status
28	│   ├── native plates/objects pane
29	│   ├── center workspace host
30	│   │   ├── existing GLCanvas3D Prepare canvas
31	│   │   └── existing G-code Preview canvas
32	│   └── wxWebView
33	│       └── local React/TypeScript Agent interface
34	├── typed workspace/controller boundary
35	├── existing Orca model, selection, plates, gizmos, and undo stack
36	└── existing slicing, project I/O, device, and print subsystems
37	```
38	
39	The boundary is deliberately conservative:
40	
41	- The viewport and overlays over the viewport remain native.
42	- The top row and object/plate pane start as native wxWidgets.
43	- C++ owns application and project state.
44	- The WebView receives versioned events and sends versioned commands.
45	- A WebView object pane may be evaluated later only as a contained presentation choice. It does not justify Electron or a WebGL viewport.
46	
47	## Authoritative ownership
48	
49	| Concern | Authoritative owner | JusPrin responsibility |
50	|---|---|---|
51	| Project model and object identity | Orca `Model` and `ObjectID` | Project a typed, session-scoped view |
52	| Plates and active plate | Orca `PartPlateList` | Present and request changes through commands |
53	| Selection and picking | Orca `Selection` and `GLCanvas3D` | Synchronize UI without feedback loops |
54	| Geometry transforms | Orca gizmos and `GizmoObjectManipulation` | Launch existing behavior and present exact values |
55	| Undo and redo | Orca undo stack | Expose availability and outcomes without a shadow stack |
56	| Slicing and Preview | Orca slicing actions and Preview canvas | Present Slice and Check print states |
57	| Project serialization | Orca 3MF and model serializers | Preserve compatibility; add migration only for new data |
58	| Agent conversation | React/TypeScript WebView | Render messages and submit typed commands |
59	| Agent print plan | C++/agent application boundary | Explain intent, decisions, uncertainty, and consequences |
60	
61	## Production integration boundaries
62	
63	### Shell host
64	
65	Use one fork-owned shell installed through one small `MainFrame` attachment. Startup policy belongs to a fork-owned bootstrap or shell factory, not to a growing collection of environment checks inside Orca constructors.
66	
67	The first production version may keep the legacy top bar, tab panel, Sidebar, and `GUI_ObjectList` constructed when existing Orca behavior depends on them. They should be excluded from the visible layout, not covered by a separate top-level window. Removing their construction is a separate lifecycle project.
68	
69	### Build registration
70	
71	Keep the explicit JusPrin source list in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/sources.cmake`. Orca's central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt` should contain one stable include rather than a growing list of fork-owned files.
72	
73	### Workspace boundary
74	
75	The production workspace API should retain the useful POC concepts: strong plate and object IDs, read-only snapshots, explicit command errors, typed change reasons, monotonic revisions, and move-only RAII subscriptions. Before production use it must also:
76	
77	- define GUI-thread requirements;
78	- define exactly when a revision advances;
79	- invalidate session IDs explicitly when a project is replaced;
80	- observe changes made outside the adapter;
81	- report history independently of widget visibility;
82	- report whether undo and redo actually changed authoritative state;
83	- avoid depending on `GUI_ObjectList` for model commands;
84	- provide plate selection, object import/addition, and other product-required commands;
85	- remain free of wxWidgets and Orca types in its public contract.
86	
87	When an operation is trapped in presentation code, expose the smallest behavior-oriented command from its current owner. Do not copy the operation into JusPrin and do not simulate input against hidden controls.
88	
89	### Canvas presentation
90	
91	Retain a product-neutral presentation API on `GLCanvas3D` and a fork-owned RAII controller that applies JusPrin policy and restores previous Orca state. Visibility and input must be independently controllable so invisible chrome cannot consume pointer events while active native gizmos remain usable.
92	
93	Production controls should be more granular than the POC's broad `render_overlays` switch. Independently classify the stock main toolbar, gizmo picker, active gizmo handles, plate actions, object labels, layer-editing controls, navigation aids, Preview legend, and Preview sliders. Shared controls such as Plater's collapse toolbar need one owner at the shell lifetime, not one guard per canvas.
94	
95	### Plates and objects pane (deferred)
96	
97	This pane remains part of the target product, but it is not part of the current
98	production-shell or Agent-WebView task and is not a prerequisite for either.
99	When it is scheduled, the production pane is intentionally smaller than
100	`GUI_ObjectList`.
101	
102	It must:
103	
104	- list and switch plates;
105	- list objects on the active plate;
106	- synchronize selection in both directions;
107	- add/import, rename, duplicate, and remove an object;
108	- expose less common operations through a selected-object menu, More, or the Agent;
109	- expand into a full tree only for multi-object, multi-part, multi-material, modifier, or print-order complexity.
110	
111	Every command must reuse Orca's snapshot, cancellation, plate-membership, selection, update, and serialization behavior.
112	
113	### Agent WebView
114	
115	The production Agent interface is a standalone local React/TypeScript package embedded in `wxWebView`. It requires:
116	
117	- a versioned command/event schema;
118	- deterministic mock conversations for UI tests;
119	- incremental message rendering and stable scroll anchoring;
120	- explicit keyboard, focus, shortcut, clipboard, selection, and IME rules;
121	- reload, startup, bridge-error, and unavailable-agent states;
122	- no direct ownership of Orca project state.
123	
124	Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. Local resource packaging must work on all three. The demonstrated prototype used a single-file local bundle to avoid WKWebView `file:` subresource failures; production may keep that approach or register an equivalent local resource scheme.
125	
126	MCP and broad agent autonomy are later layers. They must use the same typed boundary rather than changing viewport ownership.
127	
128	### Gizmo presentation
129	
130	Start with Move or Rotate and create one reusable native controller seam around existing behavior:
131	
132	1. Position a compact action strip beside the selected object.
133	2. Activate the existing native gizmo.
134	3. Preserve existing pointer manipulation, snapping, and selection.
135	4. Route exact numeric entry through `GizmoObjectManipulation`.
136	5. Preserve existing snapshot timing and undo/redo.
137	6. Dismiss without inventing a draft transaction; Undo remains the revert path unless product requirements explicitly change.
138	
139	Then convert tools by interaction family: Move/Rotate/Scale; Mirror/Duplicate/Place on face; Measure; Cut/Repair; Text/Emboss; painter-based tools.
140	
141	### Semantic annotations
142	
143	Reuse existing painter raycasting, brush selection, clipping, facet visualization, copying, undo, and 3MF persistence. The unproven production delta is arbitrary semantic labels and their agent-facing representation. The first implementation should use two labels on one object and verify save/reload, transforms, duplication, undo/redo, and behavior under topology changes before expanding the palette.
144	
145	## Non-negotiable constraints
146	
147	- Do not change slicing algorithms for UI convenience.
148	- Do not replace `GLCanvas3D` or G-code Preview.
149	- Do not reimplement geometry operations in TypeScript.
150	- Do not place WebView content over the native GL canvas.
151	- Do not create a JavaScript shadow project model or undo stack.
152	- Preserve 3MF projects, printer profiles, shortcuts, serialization, and cross-platform behavior.
153	- Do not seek stock Orca feature parity when the product definition does not require it.
154	- Do not reopen Electron or WebGL without a new explicit product decision backed by evidence.
155	
156	## Implementation order
157	
158	1. Establish canonical product documents, design tokens, and curated assets.
159	2. Productionize the workspace contract, canonical Orca commands, observation, and real-adapter tests.
160	3. Productionize the canvas presentation/controller seam.
161	4. Build the production shell without a compact object/plate pane.
162	5. Build the typed Agent WebView and bridge.
163	6. Add the Move/Rotate presentation controller and roll out gizmo families.
164	7. Add semantic annotations, Check print reporting, Send preflight, Monitor, calibration, and troubleshooting surfaces according to the product definition.
165	8. Add the compact object/plate pane as a separately planned task when it is prioritized.
166	
167	Historical implementations and detailed proof are intentionally not copied here. See [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

# How the Add a Printer flow should work on the backend

Most of this flow already exists on `jusprin-newui` (commit 39c077bff8, "Add the evidence-led Add a printer flow"). It covers the text/photo box, recognition, choosing between matches, and applying the profile. My proposal keeps that design, fills the gaps against the Figma page, and adds three shared tools so the in-app chat and external AI tools (Claude Code, Codex) can add a printer too. Some of this introduces patterns the docs don't cover yet; they're listed at the end.

I read the code on `jusprin-newui` in the main checkout. This worktree is on the old v1 branch and has no `agent-docs`.

## What exists today

- **Dialog and state machine.** [PrinterSetupController.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterSetupController.cpp) is a GUI-free state machine: Initial → Recognizing → Recognized / Ambiguous / Error → Complete.
- **The LLM call.** [PrinterRecognition.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterRecognition.cpp) makes one non-streaming OpenAI Responses call with `store:false` and a strict JSON schema. It sends:
  - the user's text and optional photo;
  - a shortlist of shipped printer profiles: up to 60 text matches, or up to 400 models when there is only a photo.

  The schema limits `candidate_ids` to that shortlist, so the model can't name a printer JusPrin doesn't ship. A test version returns fixed answers with no network call.
- **Guards.** The controller throws away any ID that wasn't offered. A single match below 0.7 confidence becomes a choice the user confirms. A correction reruns recognition with "Current match / Correction" appended to the description text.
- **Apply.** `SetupCommands::install_and_select_printer` enables the vendor/model/nozzle and selects its system preset, restoring the old setup if that fails.
- **Chat agent.** The in-app chat is separate. [OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp) runs a streaming tool loop over [ToolRegistry](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.hpp). Every change goes through `ToolExecutionCoordinator`, and the same registry feeds the MCP server that external AI tools connect to.

## Gaps against the Figma page

| Frame | Gap |
|---|---|
| 18a | Discovery reads `get_my_machine_list()`: printers already bound to the account or connected. A new printer on the LAN that isn't bound yet shows up only in `get_local_machinelist()`. |
| 18b | The assumed plate and material come back as free text. A correction like "it's on a smooth plate" is only reported as "Not applied". |
| 18c | Nothing reads nozzle, plate or AMS spools from the printer, and there is no access-code field. |
| 18d | The tell-them-apart hint ("the V2 has a knob") is squeezed into the `assumption` field. Adding a photo or more text isn't possible in the Ambiguous state, because `correct()` only works after a single match. |
| 18e | "Set it up myself" opens Orca's old wizard, not the model grid with nozzle chips. |
| 18f | I found no "No agent connected" state in the dialog. Without a key, recognition simply fails with "needs the OpenAI key". |
| Chat / MCP | There are no printer tools. An external AI tool can't add a printer. |

## Proposal

### 1. Keep the dialog as one structured call, not an agent turn

The dialog needs a fixed set of outcomes, bounded cost and latency, and a schema-checked answer. A chat tool loop gives none of those. So the dialog keeps its own recognition call. Changes to that call:

**Input.** Send the current match ID and the correction as their own labeled input parts, instead of pasting them into the description.

**Output schema, extended:**
```json
{
  "disposition": "recognized | ambiguous | no_match",
  "candidate_ids": ["<shortlist id>"],
  "evidence_summary": "string",
  "confidence": 0.0,
  "distinguishing_features": [{"candidate_id": "...", "feature": "knob under the screen"}],
  "stated_facts": {"nozzle_mm": "string|empty", "plate": "string|empty", "material": "string|empty"},
  "assumptions": [{"fact": "nozzle|plate|material", "value": "...", "reason": "..."}],
  "unresolved_correction": "string"
}
```

**Mapping the answer.** Deterministic C++, not the model, maps `stated_facts` onto real choices:
- a nozzle size picks a different shortlist ID;
- a plate maps through `SetupCommands::bed_types()`;
- a material maps through `compatible_filaments()`.

Anything that doesn't map shows as "Not applied". The model never names a preset, so it can't invent one.

**Refining an ambiguous result.** Add `refine(evidence)` to the controller for 18d. It reruns recognition with the extra text or photo, keeping the current candidates as the shortlist.

**Photo-only size (unverified).** A photo-only call can carry a 400-value enum. I believe OpenAI's structured outputs cap total enum size, but I haven't checked the exact limits. If evals show it's a problem, split it into two calls:
1. A small vision call extracts vendor, nameplate text and visible features.
2. That text builds the normal ≤60 text-match shortlist, and the existing recognition call runs on it.

Don't build the split before measuring.

### 2. Steps that need no LLM call at all

- **18c, network printer.** Map `printer_type` to the catalog entry. Then read the nozzle from `MachineObject::GetNozzleSystem()` and spools from `GetFilaSystem()`, and pick the nozzle variant that matches. The Figma copy "Nothing to assume" is literally true here. The access code goes to Orca's existing LAN-connect path and never reaches the model or any tool output. I haven't traced which Orca function performs that connect; that's the first thing to look up.
- **18e, manual setup.** A catalog query by vendor returning models and their nozzle variants, then the same apply command. "Ask the agent instead" returns to 18a.
- **18f, no agent.** The dialog checks `recognition.ready()` before rendering and shows network discovery plus manual setup. "Set up the agent" opens the Agent setup screen.

### 3. Three shared tools for the chat and MCP path

In chat, the model is itself the recognizer: it can already see image attachments. It needs no `printer_identify` tool, which would just be one LLM calling another. It needs data and one action. Following [mcp-tool-extension-guide.md](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md):

| Tool | Action | Exposure | Contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| `printers_search` | read-only | both | Input `{query, vendor?, limit ≤25, cursor?}`. Returns `{printerId: "vendor/model", vendor, model, nozzleVariants[], buildVolume, installed, current}`. IDs must be stable; today's catalog IDs are session-local and can't be reused. |
| `printers_discover` | read-only | in-app only at first | Returns model, name, connection state, nozzle and a spool summary. No IP, serial or access code. |
| `printer_setup_apply` | mutation, needs approval | both | Input `{printerId, nozzleVariant, bedType?, filamentPreset?}`. Returns the previous printer preset so the agent can offer a revert. Not part of project Undo; the result says so, like `settings_apply_patch` does. |

How the tools fit the existing rules:
- `printer_setup_apply` goes through a new `IWorkspace::select_printer` command that wraps `install_and_select_printer`. Both the dialog and the tool then use that one path, and it needs a fake-workspace implementation too.
- A pending proposal goes stale when the printer changes in the GUI, using the existing invalidation mask.
- The guide requires a failing eval before any tool is added. The eval set would include "I just got a P1S", a nameplate photo, "the ender with the touchscreen", and "I put a 0.6 nozzle on it".

### 4. Where the LLM configuration comes from

[PrinterSetupLauncher.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterSetupLauncher.cpp) reads the key itself: consent plus `load_provider_api_key("openai")`. It ignores the Agent's `enabled` and `provider` settings. Build the recognition service from `load_agent_runtime()` instead, so adding a second provider later changes one place.

## New patterns and architecture to call out

1. **A second kind of LLM call.** The architecture doc and tool guide describe only the agent tool loop. The existing printer recognition already added a one-shot structured call outside `IAgentService` and the registry, and my proposal builds on it. It should be documented as its own category ("structured task call"). Today it duplicates base64 and HTTP error mapping from the agent code. I'd extract a shared client only when a second task needs one, such as spool-photo recognition.
2. **Chaining calls**, if the two-step photo path is adopted.

Yes, both device lists are upstream OrcaSlicer, and yes, you have the direction right: a tool is code the model calls, and a tool never calls a model. The "fuzzy" part of a search belongs to the model, which turns "the small bambu one" into a concrete query. The tool itself only needs forgiving string matching, and Orca already has a matcher for that. Below, screen by screen: which steps need a model, whether that model call is doable, and which existing function supplies each piece of data.

## Your two questions

**Upstream or not.** `get_my_machine_list()` and `get_local_machinelist()` are both in OrcaSlicer v2.4.2, the commit the fork started from (8500fcdcca). No fork commit has touched `DevManager.h/.cpp` since. The fork's `PrinterDiscovery.cpp` is a 28-line wrapper around `get_my_machine_list()`.

**Fuzzy search and tools.** There are two call directions, and each screen uses one:
- **The dialog calls the model.** The app sends the user's words or photo plus the printer list, and gets back a structured answer. This is what `OpenAIPrinterRecognition` already does. It is not a tool.
- **The model calls the app.** In the chat pane, or in Claude Code or Codex over MCP, the model decides to call `printers_search("Bambu Lab A1 mini")`. The tool is plain C++ string matching. The model handles vagueness by rewriting the query and calling again.

For the string matching, Orca ships `fts::fuzzy_match` ([fts_fuzzy_match.h](src/slic3r/GUI/fts_fuzzy_match.h)), which its settings search in `Search.cpp` already uses. The tool can reuse it without changes.

The dialog may not need a search step at all. The shipped catalog is only 326 printer models from 56 vendors, 785 counting nozzle sizes. At model level, without nozzle sizes, my rough estimate is 5–7k tokens: small enough to send the whole list on every call. The current code instead picks a shortlist by matching words and lists the IDs in the schema, allowing up to 400. Sending everything and checking the returned ID in C++ is simpler, and the controller already does that check.

## Which screens need a model

| Screen | User input | Needs a model? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18a Initial | free text, or a photo | **yes** | natural-language or image identification |
| 18a "Use this" on a network printer | a click | no | the printer reports its own model ID |
| 18b Recognized, correction box | "I put a 0.6 nozzle on it" | **yes** | natural language into structured facts |
| 18c Network Selected | access code | no | device data plus Orca's connect path |
| 18d Ambiguous, "say more / add a photo" | text or photo | **yes** | same call as 18a, with the candidates narrowed |
| 18d "This one" / "Neither" | a click | no | |
| 18e Set it up myself | vendor dropdown, grid, nozzle chips | no | catalog listing |
| 18f No agent | clicks only | no | network list plus manual setup |

## The model calls, and whether each is doable

These are my assessments, not measurements. Each needs an eval set of real descriptions and photos before anyone relies on it.

1. **Text → printer model (18a, 18d).** Doable. Named models ("A1 mini", "X1C") should be reliable. Vague descriptions ("the small bambu one") should come back ambiguous, which is the designed outcome, not a failure. The model must never pick the nozzle size; C++ picks the model's default or a size the user stated.
2. **Photo → printer model (18a, 18d).** Partly doable.
   - A nameplate or a box photo is mostly text reading, so I expect it to work well.
   - A photo of the printer should work for distinctive shapes, like an enclosed P1S versus an open A1.
   - Near-identical siblings, like the Ender-3 V2 versus the V2 Neo, are uncertain.

   A photo can't show nozzle size. Photos are the least certain call and need the eval most.
3. **Correction → structured facts (18b).** Doable. The model extracts `{nozzle_mm, plate, material, accessories}`, and C++ maps each onto a real choice or reports "Not applied".
4. **"How to tell them apart" hint (18d, "the V2 has a knob").** Doable to generate, but risky. The shipped profiles contain nothing about how printers look, so the model writes this from its own knowledge and may invent a difference. Options:
   - label the hint as a suggestion;
   - drop it and ask for a photo of the front instead.

   This is a product call.

## What the app provides, and what already exists

"Upstream" means OrcaSlicer code the fork hasn't changed.

| Info or action | Screens | Existing function | Source | Wrapper needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Printer catalog: vendor, model, device model ID, nozzle sizes, default materials, unsupported bed types | 18a, 18b, 18d, 18e, tools | `VendorProfile::PrinterModel`, loaded by `PresetBundle::load_vendor_configs_from_json` (and by ConfigWizard's `BundleMap::load`) | upstream | Thin. The fork's `PrinterCatalog.cpp` (228 lines) currently re-parses the same profile JSON itself. Build volume is not on `PrinterModel`, so it still has to be read from the machine preset. I haven't checked whether `BundleMap` is reachable from outside ConfigWizard. |
| Cover image | 18b, 18c, 18e | `<vendor>/<model>_cover.png` in the profiles folder | upstream resource | none |
| Forgiving name match for a search tool | chat/MCP tool | `fts::fuzzy_match` | upstream | thin loop over the catalog |
| Printers bound to the account or connected | 18a, 18f | `DeviceManager::get_my_machine_list()` | upstream | already wrapped (`PrinterDiscovery`) |
| New LAN printers, not yet bound | 18a, 18f | `DeviceManager::get_local_machinelist()`, filled by Orca's own network discovery in `GUI_App` | upstream | same wrapper, one more loop |
| Connected device → installed preset (model plus nozzle) | 18c | `get_printer_preset(const MachineObject*)`, public in `Plater.hpp`, used by Orca's "Sync printer information" | upstream | none. It only searches **installed** system presets, so a brand-new printer must be installed first. |
| Device nozzle diameter | 18c | `GetNozzleSystem()->GetNozzles()[i].m_diameter` (zero until the printer reports it) | upstream | thin read |
| AMS spools: type, color, preset ID, loaded | 18c | `GetFilaSystem()` trays: `m_fila_type`, `color`, `setting_id`, `is_exists` | upstream | thin read, display only |
| Apply AMS spools to the project | after 18c | `Sidebar::sync_ams_list` | upstream | **not directly reusable**: it opens warning dialogs, so it can't run silently from a tool |
| Build plate from the printer | 18c | none found; `DevBed.h` has no plate type | — | The Figma copy ("Textured PEI" read from the printer) isn't backed by data. The plate would come from the profile's default bed type, so the copy should say it's assumed. |
| Access code / LAN connect | 18c | `MachineObject::set_user_access_code` (what `ConnectPrinterDialog` calls); `InputIpAddressDialog` for manual IP | upstream | thin, or open Orca's dialog |
| Install and select a printer | 18b, 18c, 18e | `PresetBundle::apply_vendor_config` → `find_system_preset_by_model_and_variant` → `Tab::select_preset` | upstream | already wrapped with rollback (`SetupCommands::install_and_select_printer`) |
| Bed type choices and selection | 18b correction | `Sidebar::set_bed_type_accord_combox` | upstream | already wrapped (`bed_types`, `select_bed_type`) |
| Compatible filaments and selection | 18b correction | Orca's `is_compatible` flag and preset-switch sequence | upstream | already wrapped (`compatible_filaments`, `select_filament_preset`) |
| Manual setup | 18e | `ConfigWizard` (what "Set it up myself" opens today) | upstream | none if the old wizard stays. The Figma grid would be catalog plus install, both already listed. |
| Model API call and key | 18a, 18b, 18d | `IAgentHttpTransport`, `load_provider_api_key` | fork | exists |

## What this means for testing

- **Everything except the three model calls already exists in upstream Orca.** Most is wrapped by the fork already; the new work is thin reads of nozzle, spool and local-printer data.
- **The two new maintenance costs** are `PrinterCatalog` duplicating Orca's profile loader, and the plate data 18c promises but the printer doesn't send.
- **Device lists without hardware.** The fork's in-process fake Bambu agent (`Testing/FakeBambuAgent`) already overrides `start_discovery` and sets an access code. It may be able to fill the local printer list without a real printer, but I haven't checked what it actually sends.
so in the add printer impl, we have llm work together with existing api calls to do text-based and iage-based search? describe how it currently works in plain eng

Not quite. Nothing in Orca does the searching. JusPrin narrows the printer list with its own simple word matching, then makes **one** OpenAI call that picks from that list. Orca's existing functions only come in at the very end, to install and select the chosen printer. There is no tool loop: the app calls the model once and reads back a structured answer.

## Step by step

**1. When the dialog opens**
- JusPrin reads the printer profile files that ship with the app (`resources/profiles/*.json`). It builds a flat list of every printer model and nozzle size: 785 entries such as "Bambu Lab A1 mini, 0.4 mm". Each entry gets a throwaway ID like `printer-12` that only lasts while the dialog is open.
- It asks Orca's device manager (`get_my_machine_list`) for printers that are online, and shows them under "Found on your network".

**2. If the user clicks "Use this" on a network printer**
- No model call. The printer reports its model code, JusPrin finds the catalog entry with the same code, and jumps straight to the confirmation screen.

**3. If the user types a description and/or drops a photo, then clicks Next**

*a. Build a shortlist.* JusPrin scores every catalog entry against the typed words:
- +3 for each shared word of 4 or more letters, +1 for shorter shared words;
- +20 if the full model name appears in the text.

If anything scores above zero, the top 60 become the shortlist, nozzle variants included. If nothing matches, which covers a photo alone or vague text like "the small one", the shortlist is instead one entry per model, up to 400.

*b. Check that the model can be used.* The user must have allowed cloud access and saved an OpenAI key in the Agent panel. If not, the dialog shows an error saying recognition needs the key, and the network list and manual setup still work.

*c. Make one OpenAI request.* It uses the Responses API, not streaming, with the model the Agent panel is set to (default `gpt-5.4-mini`). The request contains:
- instructions: identify the printer only from the user's evidence; return one printer only when the model is clearly identified; return two or three when it isn't; a photo doesn't prove nozzle size, so use the standard nozzle unless the user names one; never return an ID outside the list;
- the user's text plus the shortlist as JSON (ID, vendor, model, nozzle size, build volume, and whether it's the standard nozzle);
- the photo, if any, embedded as base64 image data;
- a strict answer format: a verdict (`recognized`, `ambiguous` or `no_match`), up to 3 IDs that must come from the shortlist, a one-line summary of the evidence, the assumption made (for example "assuming 0.4 mm nozzle"), a confidence from 0 to 1, and any part of a correction that couldn't be applied.

The request runs on a background thread, and a timer in the dialog checks for the answer. If the user starts over or retries meanwhile, any late answer to the old request is ignored.

**4. When the answer comes back**
- IDs that weren't on the shortlist, and duplicates, are thrown away.
- **One printer, verdict "recognized", confidence at least 0.7:** the "Recognized" screen (18b) shows the printer and the model's assumption text.
- **Two or more printers, or a single printer with low confidence:** the "Ambiguous" screen (18d) shows cards, and the user picks one. The app never assumes in this case.
- **Nothing usable:** an error saying the evidence didn't match a supported profile, with a pointer to manual setup.
- **HTTP errors:** a bad key is reported as not retryable; rate limits, server errors and network failures offer Retry, which repeats only the step that failed.

**5. If the user types a correction on the Recognized screen ("I put a 0.6 nozzle on it")**
- The whole request from step 3 runs again. The original text gets two added lines, "Current match: Bambu Lab A1 mini 0.4 mm nozzle" and "Correction: I put a 0.6 nozzle on it", and any photo is kept.
- If the correction can be expressed as a different catalog entry, like another nozzle size, the model returns that entry.
- Anything that can't be expressed that way, like a plate, material or accessory, comes back in the "couldn't apply" field and is shown as "Not applied".

**6. When the user clicks "Add this printer"**

`SetupCommands::install_and_select_printer` calls existing Orca functions:
1. It enables that model and nozzle size, plus its default filament, in the app config (`apply_vendor_config`).
2. It finds the matching system preset (`find_system_preset_by_model_and_variant`) and selects it in the printer settings tab.
3. It tells Orca the configuration changed.

If any step fails, it restores the previous config and the previous printer selection.

## Other paths and gaps

- **Tests and design previews** swap the OpenAI call for a fake recognizer (`DeterministicPrinterRecognition`, turned on with `JUSPRIN_PRINTER_RECOGNITION_MOCK`). It uses the same word matching and has canned answers for the Figma scenarios.
- **Text plus a photo:** the shortlist is built from the text only, so a misleading word can push the right printer off the list before the model sees the photo.
- **The "no agent connected" screen (18f)** isn't built; a missing key just shows the error from step 3b. "Set it up myself" opens Orca's old setup wizard, not the Figma model grid.

hmm, is this the best way to have llm and system calls  Work together to achieve this goal?  Let's put aside what the upstream has to offer and how we have implemented if we were implemented from scratch in the vacuum. what would be the best way to implemented given the current capability of LLMs?

Starting from scratch, I'd still use one structured model call per user action, not an agent that loops over tools. But I'd change what goes into the call and what comes out:
- **In:** the whole catalog, the printers found on the network, and the conversation so far, instead of a word-matched shortlist and pasted-together text.
- **Out:** every physical fact labeled with where it came from, not just printer IDs and a free-text assumption.

The app still does everything the model shouldn't: finding devices, checking IDs against the real catalog, choosing defaults, and installing.

None of this is measured yet. It's my design judgment about what current models are good and bad at, and it needs an eval before anyone relies on it.

## What current models change about the design

- **The catalog fits in one request.** 326 models is roughly 5–7k tokens. Pre-filtering only adds a way to lose the right answer, as when a vague phrase or a photo can't match words. Because the catalog is the same on every call, it can sit at the start of the prompt, where the provider's prompt caching makes it cheap and fast to resend.
- **Models are better at printer names than word matching is.** They know "X1C" means X1 Carbon, that "Ender 3 V2 Neo" is its own model, and that a "Combo" is a printer bundled with an AMS. So the model should choose from the real list directly.
- **Reading text in photos works well; telling look-alikes apart by shape doesn't.** Nameplates, box labels, the printer's screen and stickers are strong evidence. Telling near-identical models apart by appearance is where a model will sound sure and be wrong.
- **A model's own confidence number is not reliable.** A better signal is whether the answer quotes evidence ("the user wrote A1 mini", "the nameplate reads P1S") or was only inferred.
- **Tool loops cost time and predictability.** They pay off when the data is large, changes during the task, or is expensive to fetch. Here all the data is small and known before the call, so give it to the model up front.

## The design

**1. Collect free, reliable evidence first.** Run network discovery before the user types anything. A printer on the network reports its model, nozzle and loaded spools, which beats any guess. If exactly one new printer is found, suggest it immediately.

**2. Treat the dialog as a short conversation with one model.** Every user action is a new turn: the first description, an added photo, a correction, "neither of these", an answer to a question. Every request includes:
- a fixed prefix: instructions, then the full catalog with each model's stable ID, name, nozzle sizes and supported plates;
- the printers currently found on the network, with the data they report;
- all earlier turns, and the model's own earlier answers.

A correction is then just the next message, not text appended to the original description.

**3. The model returns the whole current state each turn,** and the app draws the screen from it:

```json
{
  "status": "identified | choose | need_more | not_in_catalog",
  "candidates": [{"model_id": "BBL/Bambu Lab A1 mini", "evidence": "user wrote 'A1 mini'",
                  "evidence_kind": "stated | read_in_photo | appearance | network_device"}],
  "question": "Is there a knob under the screen?",
  "facts": [{"fact": "nozzle_mm", "value": "0.6", "source": "stated"},
            {"fact": "accessory", "value": "AMS lite", "source": "stated"}],
  "outside_catalog": {"name": "Sovol SV08", "note": "not in the shipped profiles"}
}
```

The rules this encodes:
- **Every fact names its source.** The app only treats a fact as confirmed when it was stated, read in a photo, or reported by the device. Anything else is shown as an assumption, which matches the product rule that the user owns physical facts.
- **When unsure, ask the one question that separates the candidates, or ask for a specific photo** ("the front", "the label on the back"). Don't state how the models differ as fact; a wrong question costs one reply, while a made-up difference misleads.
- **If the printer isn't in the catalog, say what it probably is** and send the user to manual setup. Today that case is a dead end.
- **If the description matches a printer on the network,** return that device, so nozzle and spools come from the printer instead of guesses.

**4. The app checks and fills in, without the model.**
- Throw away any model ID that isn't in the catalog.
- Pick the nozzle size: stated or reported by the device, else the model's standard one.
- Map plate and material facts onto that model's actual options. Anything that doesn't map is shown as "Not applied".

The screen type comes from the answer's structure, not a confidence number. The user always clicks "Add this printer" at the end, so the model's answer can never install anything by itself.

**5. Install through the normal preset path.** Unchanged.

## Where tools belong

Tools belong in the chat pane and in external AI clients over MCP. There the model is already holding a conversation, so letting it call tools is natural. Those tools would be:
- `printers_catalog`: the catalog, optionally filtered by vendor. It's small enough that no fuzzy search is needed.
- `printers_on_network`
- `printer_add`: requires approval

Both entry points share the catalog, discovery and install code; only the direction of the calls differs.

## Compared with today's implementation

| Today | From scratch |
|---|---|
| Word-matched shortlist of 60 or 400 entries | Full catalog, cached at the start of the prompt |
| IDs for each model-and-nozzle pair, reset each time the dialog opens | Stable model IDs; the app picks the nozzle |
| Network printers kept separate from recognition | Network printers included as evidence |
| Correction pasted into the description text | Conversation turns |
| Plate and material corrections always "Not applied" | Mapped onto the chosen model's real options |
| Ambiguous screen decided by a confidence of 0.7 | Decided by the kind of evidence; the model asks a question |
| Model writes the differences as fact | Model asks a question or requests a specific photo |
| No-match is a dead end | Names the likely printer and offers manual setup |

## What has to be proven before building it

An eval set covering:
- typed names, vague descriptions, nameplate photos, box photos, front photos of look-alikes;
- corrections;
- printers that aren't in the catalog.

Measure four things:
1. how often the right printer is picked on the first answer;
2. how often the app **should** have asked but didn't (the dangerous failure);
3. how many turns it takes to finish;
4. latency and cost with the catalog cached.

The main open risk is photo-only identification of look-alike models. If the eval shows it's unreliable, the design still holds: such cases just end up asking a question or requesting a label photo more often.
What is simpler, the current implementation or your proposed design?

The current implementation is simpler. My proposal does more: it adds three screen states (ask a question, not in the catalog, printer found on the network), labels every fact with its source, and applies plate and material corrections. Each of those is new code, and the model makes more of the decisions, so more behavior has to be tested.

Some parts of the proposal, though, would make today's code **smaller** without adding any feature. Those are worth doing on their own.

## Changes that remove code

| Change | What goes away |
|---|---|
| Send the whole catalog instead of a shortlist | The word-scoring shortlist in `PrinterCatalog::recognition_choices` (~30 lines), the 60/400 split, and the bug where text pushes the right printer off the list before the model sees the photo. The strict answer format would also stop listing every allowed ID; the controller already rejects unknown IDs. |
| Stop using the confidence number to choose a screen | One branch and the 0.7 constant in `PrinterSetupController`. The user confirms before anything is installed, so the number never protected against a wrong install. |
| One catalog entry per model; C++ picks the nozzle | The prompt's nozzle rules and the per-entry "standard nozzle" flag. This moves a little logic into C++, since "I put a 0.6 nozzle on it" must map to a nozzle size, so it's closer to neutral than a pure win. |

## Changes that add code

| Change | What it adds | In the Figma design? |
|---|---|---|
| Facts labeled with their source; plate and material corrections applied | Mapping to each model's plate and filament options, plus showing them on screen | Partly: 18b shows assumptions and a correction box, but not how corrections apply |
| Network printers included in the model's evidence | Logic to merge device data with the model's answer | No |
| The model asks a question or requests a photo | A new screen state | No; 18d shows the model's description of the differences |
| "Probably X, not in the catalog" | A new screen state | No |
| Conversation turns instead of pasted text | Stored history resent on every request. About the same size as today's approach, but less fragile: the test recognizer currently has to parse the pasted "Current match:" marker. | — |

## Recommendation

Keep the current structure and make the three code-removing changes. Add the others only when an eval shows a real failure, for example users correcting the plate often, or look-alike printers getting identified wrongly. Three of the additions aren't in the Figma design at all, so building them now would mean building features nobody has asked for yet.

I've made the three changes on a new branch, `claude/printer-recognition-simplify`, cut from `jusprin-newui`. The unit tests pass. What's left is running the shell harness, which drives the real Add a printer dialog; it needs the full app built, and that build is running now.

**What changed:**
1. **The whole catalog goes to the model.** The word-matching shortlist (the 60/400 split) is deleted, and the request no longer lists every allowed ID; the controller already throws out IDs it didn't offer. The catalog now comes before the user's text, so repeated requests start the same way and the provider can cache that part.
2. **No confidence gate.** The confidence field and the 0.7 threshold are gone. The prompt now tells the model to answer "ambiguous" with one candidate when the evidence doesn't settle the model, and the dialog already shows that as a single card for the user to confirm.
3. **The app picks the nozzle.** The catalog offers one entry per model. The model only reports a nozzle size the user stated (`nozzle_mm`). The app uses that size if the model ships it, otherwise the standard nozzle, and shows an unavailable size as "Not applied: 0.6 mm nozzle".

**Things that came out differently from what I told you earlier:**
- **Not less code.** The app code is +85 / −87 lines, about the same size. The shortlist code went away, but picking and matching nozzle sizes added nearly as much back. Tests grew by 86 lines.
- **Bigger requests.** The full catalog is about 41 KB, roughly 10k tokens per request, not the 5–7k I estimated.
- **Not checked against the real OpenAI API.** No key is available in my environment, and I won't read yours out of the keychain. Whether OpenAI's strict mode accepts the new request format is unconfirmed until someone runs one real request.

**Tests:**
- Both suites passed before any edits.
- After the edits, `agent_bridge_tests` passes 171 test cases and `jusprin_tests` 48, three more than before.
- To confirm the new tests catch real bugs, I broke the nozzle reporting and the one-entry-per-model rule; 6 checks in 2 tests failed. The code is restored, byte-identical to before.
- The shell harness's fake recognizer is updated to the new format but hasn't run yet.

**Still running:** the full app and harness build, at step 142 of 720 with no errors so far. My notes say this build hit Apple's 4 GiB archive limit on this branch two days ago; if it happens again I'll relink with `llvm-ar` as recorded there. Once it builds I'll run the harness's `--printer-setup` checks. Nothing is committed yet.
